chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Abu Ayyub from Salamah said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man from us has some wealth by which he makes a living, but he has a debt. Should he feed his dependents until God, the Mighty and Majestic, brings about his ease so that he pays his debt, or should he borrow on his back (take on more debt) in the hardship of the times and the difficulty of earning, or should he accept charity?
He said: He should pay his debt with what he has, and he should not eat the wealth of people unless he has what is sufficient to return their rights to them.
Indeed, God, the Exalted, says: 'Do not consume one another's wealth unjustly, except it be trade by mutual consent from among you.'

And he should not borrow on his back unless he has the means to repay, even if he circulates among the doors of people and they turn him away with a single bite or two of food or a single date or two, unless he has a guardian who will pay after him.
And from us is one who, when he dies, God, the Mighty and Majestic, appoints for him a guardian who attends to his waiting period and his debt, and pays his waiting period and his debt.'

key_terms.عِدَتُهُ: Waiting period (for settling affairs after death)

ai.seo_question: What should a person with debt do with their available wealth according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) establishes that a debtor with available assets must prioritize settling their debt over feeding dependents, citing the Quranic prohibition against consuming wealth unjustly (4:29). He further clarifies that borrowing is permissible only if one possesses the capacity for repayment, even if it requires enduring significant hardship, and notes the Islamic legal principle that a guardian is appointed to settle the debts and waiting period of the deceased.
